title: Kufafanua mabadiliko katika muda / Describing changes over time
bridge: In Swahili, describing changes over time often involves using specific verb tenses and structures that differ from English. For instance, Swahili uses the perfect tense to describe actions that started in the past and continue into the present, whereas English might use the present perfect continuous. Additionally, Swahili relies heavily on context and verb prefixes to indicate time, which can be a trap for English speakers who are used to more explicit time markers like 'since' or 'for'.
rule: To describe changes over time in Swahili, use the perfect tense (formed with the prefix me-/me- for most verbs) to indicate actions that began in the past and have relevance to the present. For ongoing changes, the present continuous tense (na ku-) is used. For completed changes, the simple past tense (ali-) is appropriate. Be mindful of verb prefixes that change based on the subject and tense. For example, 'nimeliona' (I have seen) vs. 'naliona' (I was seeing).

concept_examples.text: Nimelijua Kiswahili kwa miaka miwili.
concept_examples.translation: I have been learning Swahili for two years.

concept_examples.text: Bijani zimeongezeka sana katika mji wetu.
concept_examples.translation: Businesses have increased a lot in our town.

concept_examples.text: Alipokuja hapa, alikuwa mtu mmoja tu.
concept_examples.translation: When he came here, he was just one person.

concept_examples.text: Sasa nina kazi njema zaidi kuliko mwaka uliopita.
concept_examples.translation: Now I have a better job than last year.
concept_examples.phonetic: /sa.sa nɪ.na ka.zi n.dʒɛ.ma zɛɪ.di ku.lɪ.kɔ m.wa.ka u.lɪ.ʔɔ.pɪ.ta/

common_error.wrong: Nimelijua Kiswahili kwa miaka miwili sasa.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often add 'sasa' (now) unnecessarily when describing ongoing changes, as the perfect tense in Swahili already implies present relevance. The correct sentence omits 'sasa' because the tense itself conveys the continuity.

examples.translation: I have started doing exercises every morning.
examples.note: Use the perfect tense to describe a new habit that continues into the present.

examples.translation: Businesses have increased a lot.
examples.note: Highlight the change using the perfect tense with 'zimeongezeka'.

examples.translation: I have moved to a big city.
examples.note: Describe a significant life change using the perfect tense.

examples.original: Alipokuja hapa, alikuwa mtu mmoja tu.
examples.translation: When he came here, he was just one person.
examples.note: Contrast past and present using the simple past tense.

examples.original: Teknolojia imebadilika sana katika miaka ya hivi karibuni.
examples.phonetic: /tɛ.kɔ.nɔ.lɔ.dʒɪ.a ɪ.mɛ.ba.dɪ.lɪ.ka sa.na ka.tɪ.ka mɪ.a.ka ja hɪ.vi ka.ɾɪ.bu.ni/
examples.translation: Technology has changed a lot in recent years.
examples.note: Describe broad societal changes using the perfect tense.

examples.original: Watu wengi zaidi wanatumia simu za kiuchumi sasa.
examples.phonetic: /wa.tu wɛŋ.gi zɛɪ.di wa.na.tu.mɪ.a sɪ.mu za kɪ.u.tʃu.mi sa.sa/
examples.translation: More people use smartphones now.
examples.note: Indicate a trend using the present tense with 'sasa'.

title: Kufikiri na kufanya makusanyiko / Speculating and Making Deductions
bridge: In Swahili, speculating and making deductions often involve specific verb forms and expressions that differ from English. For instance, Swahili uses the verb 'kufikiri' (to think) with conditional clauses, whereas English might use 'must' or 'probably'. Be cautious of literal translations; 'lazima' (must) in Swahili is stronger than its English counterpart and implies certainty rather than speculation.
rule: To speculate or make deductions in Swahili, use the following structures: 1) 'Pengine' (maybe) + verb in present tense for possibilities. 2) 'Lazima' (must) + verb in present tense for strong deductions. 3) 'Kama' (if) + conditional clause for hypothetical situations. Note that 'kufikiri kwamba' (to think that) is used to express thoughts or beliefs, similar to 'I think that' in English.

concept_examples.text: Pengine yuko nyumbani.
concept_examples.translation: Maybe he/she is at home.

concept_examples.text: Lazima ameenda kazini.
concept_examples.translation: He/she must have gone to work.

concept_examples.text: Kama yale yaliyoongezeka, lazima bei imeongezeka.
concept_examples.translation: If those increased, the price must have increased.

concept_examples.text: Nafikiri kwamba ataeza.
concept_examples.translation: I think that he/she is coming.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often misuse 'pengine' (maybe) with past tense verbs, which is incorrect in Swahili. 'Pengine' should be used with present tense for possibilities, while 'lazima' (must) is used for strong deductions about past actions.

examples.translation: Maybe he/she will come tomorrow.
examples.note: Use 'pengine' with present tense for possibilities.

examples.translation: Maybe it's the sun.
examples.note: Simple speculation about a current situation.

examples.translation: He/she must be at home.
examples.note: Use 'lazima' for strong deductions about present or past actions.

examples.translation: He/she must have arrived.
examples.note: Deduction about a past action based on evidence.

examples.translation: If those increased, the price has increased.
examples.note: Use 'kama' for hypothetical situations with conditional clauses.

examples.translation: If he/she is at home, he/she must have returned.
examples.note: Combining 'kama' with 'lazima' for complex deductions.

title: Kusema Hasira na Kutafakari / Expressing Regret and Hypothetical Situations
bridge: In Swahili, expressing regret and hypothetical situations involves specific structures that differ from English. Unlike English, which uses 'if' clauses and modal verbs like 'would' or 'could', Swahili uses conditional particles like 'la' or 'anga' to convey hypothetical scenarios. Additionally, Swahili often omits the subject pronoun when the context is clear, which can be a trap for English speakers who are used to explicit subjects. Be mindful of word order and the placement of conditional markers.
rule: To express regret, Swahili uses the past tense with the particle 'la' to indicate a missed opportunity or a wish that something had happened differently. For hypothetical situations, the particle 'anga' is used in the past tense to describe unreal or imagined scenarios. The structure is: Subject + anga + verb (past tense). Note that 'anga' is placed before the verb, unlike English where 'if' typically starts the clause. For present or future hypotheticals, 'la' can also be used with the present tense to express a condition.

concept_examples.text: Ningelikuwa nikiwa na pesa, ningelipata gari.
concept_examples.translation: If I had money, I would buy a car.
concept_examples.phonetic: nɪŋɡɛlɪkuwa nɪkiwa na pesa, nɪŋɡɛlɪpata ɡari

concept_examples.text: La ningelipoenda shule, ningelifanya vizuri.
concept_examples.translation: If I had gone to school, I would have done well.

concept_examples.text: Anga nipate kazi, nitaweka bidii.
concept_examples.translation: If I got a job, I would work hard.

concept_examples.text: La nikingewea, singekuwa na tatizo.
concept_examples.translation: If I had prepared, I wouldn’t have had a problem.

common_error.wrong: If niko na pesa, nitakanuza gari.
common_error.correct: La ningelikuwa na pesa, ningelipata gari.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'if' without using the correct conditional particles 'la' or 'anga'. Additionally, they may use the present tense instead of the past tense for hypothetical situations. Remember to use 'la' or 'anga' and adjust the verb tense accordingly.

examples.translation: If I had gone to school, I would have done well.
examples.note: Use 'la' with the past tense to express regret about a missed opportunity.

examples.translation: If I had prepared, I wouldn’t have had a problem.
examples.note: Combine 'la' with the past tense to express a hypothetical past situation.

examples.translation: If I got a job, I would work hard.
examples.note: Use 'anga' with the past tense to describe a realistic hypothetical scenario.

examples.original: La ningelikuwa na pesa, ningelipata gari.
examples.phonetic: la nɪŋɡɛlɪkuwa na pesa, nɪŋɡɛlɪpata ɡari
examples.translation: If I had money, I would buy a car.
examples.note: Combine 'la' with the past tense to express a condition in the past.

examples.translation: If I knew, I would have come.
examples.note: Use 'anga' to express a hypothetical statement in the past.

examples.translation: If I could, I would help.
examples.note: Use 'la' with the present tense to express a hypothetical condition in the present.

title: Kufahamu Mahali Pa Kutoa na Kupokea / Understanding Pros and Cons
bridge: In Swahili, discussing advantages and disadvantages often involves more explicit expressions of comparison than in English. While English might use 'on the one hand... on the other hand,' Swahili uses phrases like 'kwa upande mmoja' and 'kwa upande wa pili' to structure the discussion. Be cautious not to directly translate English phrases like 'pros and cons' as Swahili tends to be more descriptive and contextual.
rule: To discuss advantages and disadvantages in Swahili, use the structure 'Kwa upande mmoja, [advantage], lakini kwa upande wa pili, [disadvantage].' For expressing opinions, phrases like 'ninaona kwamba' (I think that) or 'ni jambo la kufurahia' (it's something to be happy about) are common. Avoid literal translations of English idioms; instead, focus on clear, descriptive language.

concept_examples.text: Kwa upande mmoja, kujifunza Kiswahili ni jambo la kufurahia, lakini kwa upande wa pili, ni jambo la kushindwa.
concept_examples.translation: On one hand, learning Swahili is something to be happy about, but on the other hand, it's challenging.
concept_examples.phonetic: /kwa upande mmoja, kujifunza kiswahili ni jambo la kufurahia, lakini kwa upande wa pili, ni jambo la kushindwa/

concept_examples.text: Ninaona kwamba kuwepo kwa mazingira mazuri ni kitu cha maana, lakini pia inaweza kuwa na tatizo la kutosha.
concept_examples.translation: I think that having a good environment is important, but it can also have insufficient problems.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ninaona kwamba kuwepo kwa mazingira mazuri ni kitu cha maana, lakini pia inaweza kuwa na tatizo la kutosha/

concept_examples.text: Kwa upande mmoja, kufanya michezo ni jambo la kufurahia, lakini kwa upande wa pili, inaweza kuwa na hatari.
concept_examples.translation: On one hand, playing sports is enjoyable, but on the other hand, it can be dangerous.
concept_examples.phonetic: /kwa upande mmoja, kufanya michezo ni jambo la kufurahia, lakini kwa upande wa pili, inaweza kuwa na hatari/

common_error.wrong: Ni vizuri sana na ni mbaya sana.
common_error.correct: Kwa upande mmoja, ni vizuri sana, lakini kwa upande wa pili, ni mbaya sana.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'very good and very bad' without the necessary contrastive structure. Swahili requires explicit comparison using 'kwa upande mmoja' and 'kwa upande wa pili' to clearly discuss both sides.

examples.original: Kwa upande mmoja, ni jambo la kufurahia, lakini kwa upande wa pili, ni jambo la kushindwa.
examples.phonetic: /kwa upande mmoja, ni jambo la kufurahia, lakini kwa upande wa pili, ni jambo la kushindwa/

examples.note: Use this structure to introduce basic pros and cons.

examples.original: Ninaona kwamba ni jambo la maana, lakini pia inaweza kuwa na tatizo.
examples.phonetic: /ninaona kwamba ni jambo la maana, lakini pia inaweza kuwa na tatizo/

examples.translation: For example, learning a new language is enjoyable, but it can take time.
examples.note: Add examples using 'kwa mfano' to support your points.

examples.original: Ninaona kwamba ni jambo la kufurahia, lakini ni lazima tuwe makini na hatari zilizopo.

examples.note: Acknowledge different perspectives using 'kwa wengine' for a nuanced discussion.

title: Kusimamia hadithi / Narrating a story
bridge: In Swahili, narrating a story involves a more direct and concise style compared to English. While English often uses complex sentence structures and connectors, Swahili relies on simpler sentences and context. Be cautious of overusing English-style connectors like 'and then' or 'because,' as Swahili often omits them. Additionally, Swahili uses a different tense system, so avoid directly translating English tenses.
rule: To narrate a story in Swahili, use the past tense for completed actions and the present tense for ongoing or habitual actions. The past tense is formed by adding the prefix -li- to the verb stem (e.g., nili- for 'I'). For sequential events, use the conjunction na (and) sparingly, as Swahili often relies on context. Avoid overusing connectors like kisha (then) unless necessary for clarity. Remember, Swahili storytelling is more straightforward, focusing on actions rather than complex explanations.

concept_examples.text: Jana nilienda kwenye biashara na nikakuta rafiki yangu.
concept_examples.translation: Yesterday I went to the market and found my friend.

concept_examples.text: Kwa kushangaa, yule mwanamke aliondoka kwa haraka.

concept_examples.phonetic: ˈkwa ˈkushangaa, ˈyule ˈmwanamke ˈaliondoka ˈkwa ˈharaka.

common_error.correct: Jana nilienda kwenye biashara na nikakuta rafiki yangu.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often overuse 'kisha' (then) when narrating stories in Swahili. While 'kisha' is correct, Swahili typically relies on context and simpler sentence structures. Avoid adding unnecessary connectors unless they enhance clarity.

examples.original: Hapo zamani, kulikuwa na mwanamke mmoja.

examples.translation: In the end, that woman returned home.

examples.translation: That's how the story ended.

title: Kutoa maoni / Arguing a Point of View
bridge: In Swahili, arguing a point of view often involves a more indirect and respectful approach compared to English. While English speakers might use strong, direct statements like 'I disagree,' Swahili speakers tend to soften their arguments with phrases like 'Nafikiri kwamba...' (I think that...) or 'Si kama...' (It's not like...). Be cautious not to overuse direct contradictions, as they can come across as confrontational in Swahili.
rule: To argue a point of view in Swahili, use expressions like 'Nafikiri kwamba...' (I think that...), 'Si kama...' (It's not like...), or 'Lakini...' (But...) to introduce your opinion. Follow these with clear reasoning or examples. Avoid overly direct contradictions like 'Hiyo si kweli' (That's not true) unless you want to be more assertive. Remember to maintain a polite tone, especially in formal or unfamiliar settings.

concept_examples.text: Nafikiri kwamba hiyo si jambo la kufanya.
concept_examples.translation: I think that’s not something to do.
concept_examples.phonetic: nafikiri kwamba hiyo si jambo la kufanya

concept_examples.text: Si kama ulivyosema, kuna sababu nyingine.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly state 'That's not true' in Swahili as 'Hiyo si kweli,' which can sound too blunt. Instead, use 'Nafikiri kwamba hiyo si kweli' or 'Si kama ulivyosema' to soften the argument and maintain politeness.

examples.translation: I think that...
examples.note: Use this phrase to introduce your opinion gently.

examples.translation: It's not like you said.

examples.translation: Because...
examples.note: Use this to explain your reasoning clearly.

examples.translation: That’s how I see it.

examples.note: Encourages further reflection without being confrontational.

title: Kuhusu Kazi / Talking about Work
bridge: In Swahili, discussing work and careers often involves more contextual and relational language compared to English. For instance, Swahili speakers frequently use verbs that imply ongoing effort or collaboration, whereas English might use more direct verbs. Be cautious of false friends like 'kazini' (at work) vs. 'in work' in English, which has a different connotation.
rule: To talk about work in Swahili, use the verb 'kufanya kazi' (to work) or 'kushughulikia' (to deal with). When describing roles, use 'ni' (I am) followed by the profession, e.g., 'Ni mwalimu' (I am a teacher). For locations, use 'kazini' (at work) or 'ofisini' (at the office). Remember, Swahili often emphasizes the activity or relationship rather than just the role, so phrases like 'ninashughulikia' (I deal with) are common.

title: Jinsi ya kufanya / Describing Processes
bridge: In Swahili, describing processes often involves using the verb 'kufanya' (to do) in a more structured way than in English. Unlike English, where we might use simple present or past tense, Swahili uses a specific construction with 'ku-' (infinitive marker) and '-a' (present tense suffix) to describe steps in a process. Be cautious of word order, as Swahili typically follows a subject-verb-object structure, which can differ from English.
rule: To describe a process in Swahili, use the verb 'kufanya' followed by the infinitive of the action. The structure is: 'Kufanya [action] + [details]'. For sequential steps, use 'kwa kufanya' (by doing) or 'baada ya kufanya' (after doing). Remember, Swahili verbs are regular and do not change based on the subject, unlike English. Use time markers like 'kwanza' (first), 'baada ya hapo' (after that), and 'mwishowe' (finally) to sequence steps.

concept_examples.text: Kufanya chakula ni jambo rahisi.
concept_examples.translation: Making food is easy.

concept_examples.text: Kwa kufanya mazoezi kila siku, utafikia malengo yako.
concept_examples.translation: By exercising every day, you will achieve your goals.
concept_examples.phonetic: /kwa kuˈfanya maˈzoezi ˈkila ˈsiku, uˈtafikia maˈlengo ˈjako/

concept_examples.text: Baada ya kufanya kazi, ninaenda nyumbani.

concept_examples.text: Kufanya safari inahitaji mawazo mema.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'do' to 'kufanya' without considering the infinitive structure. In Swahili, 'to make food' is 'kuandaa chakula' or 'kuchambua chakula,' not 'kufanya chakula.' Always use the correct infinitive form after 'ku-'.

title: Kushughulikia wasiwasi / Expressing Uncertainty
bridge: In Swahili, expressing uncertainty often involves specific modal verbs and structures that differ from English. For instance, Swahili uses 'hujaa' (it's not clear) or 'si sure' (I'm not sure) instead of English phrases like 'I think' or 'maybe'. Be cautious not to directly translate English expressions, as Swahili has its own idiomatic ways to convey doubt or probability.
rule: To express uncertainty in Swahili, use modal verbs like 'kuweza' (to be able to) in a questioning or speculative manner, or phrases like 'si sure' (I'm not sure) and 'hujaa' (it's not clear). For probability, use 'inaweza' (it can) or 'labda' (maybe). Avoid direct translations from English; instead, focus on Swahili-specific constructions. For example, 'I think' in English translates to 'nayo' (I also) in a speculative context, not a direct equivalent.

concept_examples.text: Si sure kama atakuja.
concept_examples.translation: I'm not sure if he will come.

concept_examples.text: Labda ni kweli.
concept_examples.translation: Maybe it's true.

concept_examples.text: Inaweza kuwa kweli.
concept_examples.translation: It could be true.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'I think' into Swahili, which sounds unnatural. Instead, use 'nayo' (I also) in a speculative context or 'labda' (maybe) to express uncertainty more idiomatically in Swahili.

examples.translation: I'm not sure.

examples.note: 'Labda' is a common way to express uncertainty or possibility.

examples.translation: It might be.
examples.note: 'Kuweza kuwa' is another way to convey possibility.

examples.translation: I think he will come.
examples.note: Use 'nayo' in a speculative context to express a hypothesis.

examples.translation: If it's true.
examples.note: 'Ikiwa ni kweli' introduces a conditional hypothesis.

examples.translation: Although I'm not sure.
examples.note: Use 'ingawa' to introduce a contrasting hypothesis.

title: Kutoa ombi rasmi / Making Formal Requests
bridge: In Swahili, formal requests often use the verb 'kuomba' (to ask) or 'kutaka' (to want), followed by the object of the request. Unlike English, where 'please' is commonly placed at the end of a sentence, in Swahili, 'tafadhali' (please) typically comes at the beginning or end of the sentence. Be cautious not to overuse 'kuomba' in informal settings, as it may sound overly formal. Additionally, Swahili formal requests often include a polite introductory phrase, which is less common in English.
rule: To make a formal request in Swahili, use the structure: 'Nataka [object]' or 'Ninataka [object]' for 'I want [object]', or 'Nakuomba [object]' for 'I ask you for [object]'. Always include 'tafadhali' (please) for politeness. For written requests, start with a formal greeting like 'Hallo' or 'Shikamoo' (for elders) and end with 'Asante' (thank you). Remember, the verb conjugation changes based on the subject and object, so pay attention to agreement.

concept_examples.text: Nataka kitabu hicho, tafadhali.
concept_examples.translation: I would like that book, please.

concept_examples.text: Nakuomba msaada, tafadhali.
concept_examples.translation: I ask you for help, please.

concept_examples.text: Ninataka kufanya mtihani wa kwanza, tafadhali.
concept_examples.translation: I would like to take the first exam, please.

concept_examples.text: Hallo, ninataka kuwasiliana na mkuu wa ofisi, tafadhali.
concept_examples.translation: Hello, I would like to speak with the head of the office, please.
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈhalo, ninˈataka kuwasilɪˈana na mˈkuu wa oˈfisi, taˈfadhali

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'please' instead of using 'tafadhali'. Additionally, placing 'please' at the end of the sentence is less common in Swahili. Always use 'tafadhali' and place it appropriately for a natural sound.

examples.translation: I would like water, please.
examples.note: Use 'nataka' for simple, direct requests.

examples.translation: Please, I ask for help.
examples.note: Place 'tafadhali' at the beginning for emphasis.

examples.original: Nataka kufanya mtihani wa kwanza, tafadhali.
examples.phonetic: ninˈataka kuˈfanya mtɪˈhani wa kˈwanza, taˈfadhali
examples.translation: I would like to take the first exam, please.
examples.note: Add details like 'mtikhani wa kwanza' (first exam) for specificity.

examples.original: Nakuomba taarifa zaidi kuhusu huduma hizi.
examples.phonetic: naˈkuomba taˈarifa ˈzidi kuhusu ˈhuduma ˈhizi
examples.translation: I ask for more information about these services.
examples.note: Use 'taarifa zaidi' (more information) for detailed requests.

examples.translation: Thank you for your help.
examples.note: End with 'asante' (thank you) for politeness.

examples.original: Nataka kujua iwapo unaweza kusaidia, tafadhali.
examples.phonetic: naˈtaka kuˈdʒua iwapo uˈnaweza kuˈsaɪdɪa, taˈfadhali
examples.translation: I would like to know if you can help, please.
examples.note: Use 'kujua iwapo' (to know if) for conditional requests.
